water quality, quantity and reliability were all poor in the study slum, and that water contamination in this setting is largely due to poor storage and treatment practices, and to some extent, point-of-source contamination.
the informal water distribution system we evaluated was associated with poor quality, inadequate quantity, high cost and poor reliability of water.
water insecurity in this slum is characterized by severe water quality and quantity problems that are not adequately addressed by existing interventions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social ecology of water and the social determinants of water-related disease in urban slums.

the health and social inequity of water in a slum, but also with the social ecology of water, as it is influenced by the physical environment, the distribution system, and the social environment of a slum community.
the social and ecological dimensions of water in the urban slums of Mumbai, India.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the slum water system is a failed system.
water insecurity in this slum is due to a combination of factors: inadequate quantity of water; poor water quality at point of source and during storage in the home; and exorbitant expense.
water quality and quantity is a major issue in the slums of Mumbai and that the government needs to address the problem.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social ecology of water is not conducive to safe drinking water in this slum.
water is a human rights issue in Mumbai.
the slum community is not getting a fair share of the water supply and that they are paying too much for water.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lack of access to safe water in Mumbai slums is a public health problem that requires urgent attention.
slum residents should be given legal access to municipal supplies, which will reduce the burden of unsafe water on households and the government.
slum water systems should be considered as a public health priority, as they are a major source of water-borne disease in urban India and elsewhere.
